title: Fewest Bookings to Cancel
statement:
A single studio has a list of booking requests, bookings[i] = [start, end], with start < end. Two bookings clash when their times overlap. A booking that ends exactly when another starts, like [2, 5] and [5, 8], does not clash.

Return the smallest number of bookings to cancel so that no two of the remaining bookings clash.

examples.why: [4, 7] is the shortest booking, but it clashes with both others. Keeping it forces two cancellations; cancelling just it keeps [1, 5] and [6, 10].
Sorting by start and keeping the first booking keeps [1, 10], which blocks both others. Cancel it instead.
[3, 6] and [6, 9] only touch, so both can stay. The duplicate [3, 6] has to go.

hints: Cancelling as few as possible is the same as keeping as many as possible. Which booking would you keep first?
Shortest-first and earliest-start-first both fail (examples 1 and 2). Think about what a kept booking costs you: the time after it that is still free.
Sort by end time. Keep a booking whenever it starts at or after the end of the last kept one; otherwise cancel it. The booking that ends first leaves the most room for everything after it.

explain.intuition:
Flip the question: cancel as few as possible means keep as many as possible without clashes. That is the classic activity selection problem, and the greedy rule is: among the bookings that still fit, keep the one that ends earliest.

Why does that work? Take any best set of kept bookings and look at its first one. Swap it for the booking that ends earliest overall. That booking ends no later, so it cannot clash with anything the best set kept afterwards. The set is still valid and the same size. Repeat the argument after that booking and you rebuild a best answer that is exactly the greedy one. Earliest start fails because a long booking can start first (example 2), and shortest fails because a short booking can sit across two others (example 1). Only the end time measures how much of the future a booking uses up.
steps: For each booking [s, e]: if s ≥ lastEnd, keep it and set lastEnd = e.
Otherwise it clashes with a kept booking that ends no later than it does: cancel it, cancelled++.
pitfalls: Sorting by start and always keeping the earlier booking. Example 2 keeps [1, 10] and loses two.
Using s > lastEnd. Bookings that only touch do not clash, so example 3 would cancel two instead of one.
Counting clashing pairs instead of bookings to cancel. One long booking can clash with many short ones and still only needs one cancellation.

solutions.title: Dynamic programming over end times
solutions.idea: Sort by end. best[i] is the most bookings you can keep if booking i is the last one kept: 1 plus the best over earlier bookings that end by its start.

solutions.title: Greedy by earliest end
solutions.idea: Sort by end. Keep each booking that starts at or after the last kept end; cancel the rest.

followups: Each booking now pays a different amount, and you want to keep the most money, not the most bookings. Why does the greedy break, and what replaces it?
Return which bookings to cancel, not only how many.
